title: The Main Story: The Fraud Task Force Would Rather You Didn't Ask About the $420 Million Prison
dek: The administration came to Minnesota to hunt fraud. It leaves behind a $495.6 million prison the state was offered for $75 million, a watchdog report with “waste” in the title, two dead citizens, and a Treasury secretary who called the question a waste of his time.
body:
## A banner, a podium and an empty chair

Our main story tonight is fraud. Specifically, the federal government's war on it, which this week arrived in St. Cloud, Minnesota, in the form of the Treasury secretary, the FBI director and the man who runs Medicare, standing in a police station in front of a banner that read "The Vice President's Fraud Task Force" [2][4]. The vice president was not there. He canceled the night before, without giving a reason, which left three of the most powerful officials in the country standing under a sign with somebody else's name on it, like a wedding band playing a reception the groom skipped [2][4].

They had news. The FBI had served 17 search warrants and charged four Medicaid providers with stealing about $41 million, and Dr. Mehmet Oz held up the case of a woman convicted earlier this month in a housing program the state itself had already shut down [2][3]. These are real cases and real money, and if the task force wanted to stop there, fine. It did not want to stop there. Scott Bessent said fraud was all over the entire state and that the governor had turned a blind eye to it [2]. Oz said the whole national anti-fraud effort started right here in Minnesota [2]. Minnesota, in this telling, is not a state. It is a crime scene with lakes.

Then Lou Raguse of KARE 11 asked a question. He noted that the administration had declared war on waste and fraud, and asked whether the secretary could explain the $420 million the federal government had just paid above the asking price for a prison in Appleton, Minnesota [3][4]. And Scott Bessent, Secretary of the Treasury of the United States, keeper of the nation's checkbook, said: yeah, he didn't know anything about that [3][4]. The task force was there to prosecute criminal fraud, he said, and a question like that, one that deflects from it, "is a waste of our time" [4].

Which is a fascinating thing to say about $420 million. Because that is a lot of our time.

## The building

Here is the building. The Prairie Correctional Facility in Appleton, a small town in west-central Minnesota about three hours from the Twin Cities. It has 1,600 beds. It has been empty since 2010, which means it has spent sixteen years doing what most of us do on a Sunday: nothing, at scale [5][7]. (The Watch has the full account in [its report on the sale](https://bboldt86.github.io/lanscape-navigator/news/#/a/2026-10-31-ice-paid-495-million-for-appleton-prison-offered-for-75) and [an analysis of the year's record](https://bboldt86.github.io/lanscape-navigator/news/#/a/2026-10-31-minnesota-fraud-hunters-ledger-two-dead-citizens-420-million-prison).)

Its owner is CoreCivic, the private prison company, and CoreCivic has been trying to sell this building for a very long time. In May 2025 it offered the prison to the State of Minnesota for $75 million, upgrades included, which the state's Department of Corrections confirmed this week [1][5]. Minnesota passed. Officials did not want to staff a remote site with 500 people they would also have to build housing for [5]. Swift County, which sends the tax bill, values the whole property at $14.75 million [6].

Fifteen months later, on August 4 of this year, the United States of America, acting through the Department of Homeland Security, bought it for $495.6 million [8]. Signed and closed the same day [8]. Six and a half times what the state was asked to pay. Thirty-three times what the county says it is worth. KARE 11 calls it the most expensive property purchase in Minnesota's history, which is a remarkable thing to be able to say about a building nobody else wanted at a tenth of the price [16].

Paul Schnell, the corrections commissioner who received the $75 million offer, said he was stunned, said it was unexplainable, and said he still cannot figure it out [16][4]. Paul, you are not alone. Nobody can figure it out, because nobody will show their work.

## A cost-based methodology

CoreCivic has an explanation, and it is my favorite kind: the kind that is technically a sentence. A spokesperson told KARE 11 that independent appraisers used a cost-based methodology and that "the federal government ultimately determined the sale price following its assessment process" [5]. Nobody has released the appraisal. DHS and ICE did not answer when reporters asked how the number was reached [5][6].

When it sold two California prisons to the same buyer in July, CoreCivic described the method: an appraisal built on replacement cost, depreciation and land value [17]. A cost-based appraisal, for those of you who have never bought a prison, asks what it would cost to build the thing from scratch today. It does not ask what anyone would actually pay. By that logic my 2009 Corolla is worth $34,000 because that is what a new one costs, and I would like the federal government to know that it is available, same-day close.

And the terms get better. CoreCivic does not leave the building. It keeps running it for ICE under a five-year contract through 2031, for which it expects about $75 million a year, a flat monthly fee plus a daily rate per detainee [7]. So the company sold the prison for $495 million and will be paid the prison's entire old asking price, every year, to keep standing in it. On the same day the sale was signed, CoreCivic's board raised its stock buyback authority to $755.8 million, and six days later the company spent $500 million of cash buying back its own shares [9]. The company had told investors the sale money could go toward paying down debt and buying back stock, and within a week it had bought back roughly a prison's worth [8][9].

CoreCivic also gave $500,000 to the inaugural committee and spent $1.77 million lobbying on the budget law that paid for all of this, according to Bring Me The News [6]. I am not saying there is a connection. I am saying that if you wanted to draw one, you would not need a very long crayon.

## What else the fraud money bought

That budget law gave ICE $45 billion through 2029 to expand detention, against about $3.8 billion in ordinary appropriations last year, so Appleton is not a one-off. It is a sample [11]. In July the government bought two more CoreCivic prisons in California for $739 million and $733 million; Appleton and a Leavenworth, Kansas, facility followed in August, about $2.2 billion for four prisons in one summer [17][8][5]. The San Diego one, Otay Mesa, is assessed at $160 million [6].

Then there are the warehouses. ICE bought eleven of them for $1.07 billion to turn into detention centers, and by June it was trying to sell seven, which had cost $707 million, having spent more than $20 million on zoning, security and electricity it will never get back [10][11]. You know who looked at all of this? The Government Accountability Office, the federal government's own auditor, which in September released a report titled "Urgent Planning Needed to Avoid Further Waste of Taxpayer Dollars" [10]. That is not a headline a critic wrote. That is the title. The GAO found that ICE had no strategic plan for the expansion, had not weighed expensive facilities against cheaper ones it already had, and did not know whether it could afford what it was buying [10][11]. DHS agreed with all of that and promised a plan. The plan is due August 31, 2027 [10]. So the agency spending $45 billion will tell us what it is for roughly two years after it started spending it, like a man who buys a boat and then takes a course on whether he likes water.

Now, I want to be precise here, because the task force is very big on precision when the defendant is a home-care company. Nobody has alleged that the Appleton purchase broke a law. The attorney general of Minnesota calls it scamming taxpayers out of almost half a billion dollars and has asked three congressional committees to look [5][6]. The government's auditor calls the program waste [10]. CoreCivic calls it the result of an assessment process [5]. And the Treasury secretary calls the question a waste of his time [4]. Four descriptions, no appraisal, and a $420 million gap that, as the KARE 11 reporters pointed out, is bigger than the estimated loss in Feeding Our Future, the scandal that this entire roadshow exists to invoke [16][2].

## The other thing that happened in Minnesota

Because here is where the joke stops, and it has to, because the fraud story was never only about money.

The administration cited Minnesota's fraud scandals to justify sending thousands of federal immigration agents into the state last winter, and no one arrested in that operation was ever charged with fraud [2]. A CBS News analysis of the government's own records counted about 3,800 arrests; 24 percent had a criminal conviction, 63 percent were arrested for nothing but an immigration violation, the largest group was from Ecuador, and Somali nationals, the people the president had singled out, were under 3 percent [12][2].

The operation killed two people. Both were American citizens. Renee Good, 37, a mother of three, was shot through her windshield by an ICE officer on January 7 as she left a protest, and the Associated Press's analysis of the video shows him firing twice more from about an arm's length away [13]. Alex Pretti, 37, an intensive-care nurse, was killed on January 24 while filming Border Patrol agents; ABC News reconstructed it from six videos, and the sequence runs pepper spray, dragged by his hood, pinned, punched, his handgun removed from his waistband, and then ten shots in under five seconds, the first about one second after the gun was taken [14]. The Homeland Security secretary said that day that he had come to kill law enforcement [14].

Ten months later no one has been charged in either death [13]. Minnesota had to sue the federal government for the evidence; the government started handing it over in July and then stopped in September, citing "challenges with D.C.," and as of last week it still held Good's clothing, the phone of the officer who shot her, the recorded statement of the officer who shot Pretti, the guns and the casings [13]. The Justice Department's position is that sharing is at its discretion [13].

And the one agent charged over a shooting, for wounding a man in the leg and allegedly lying about it, is sitting in a Texas jail because Governor Greg Abbott will not sign the extradition papers until Minnesota, in his words, steps up and does what is right, by which he means its fraud problem [15]. Read that twice. Fraud is now the reason a man charged with shooting someone and lying about it does not have to show up to court.

## The receipts

So let's total the ledger the way the task force would if the task force were pointed the other direction. On one side: four Medicaid providers, $41 million alleged, seventeen warrants, a cabinet secretary, the FBI director, the head of Medicare, a banner, a podium [2][3]. On the other: one empty prison, $420 million over asking, no appraisal, a buyback, a donor, two dead citizens, a shrink-wrapped car in an FBI warehouse and a federal watchdog using the word waste in the title [1][9][10][13][18].

I believe fraud is bad. I believe billing Medicaid for a client who is at a funeral is bad, and a jury should decide it [3]. I also believe that a government which calls that fraud, and calls paying six and a half times the asking price for a building an assessment process, has not declared war on fraud. It has declared war on a definition, and the definition is losing.

Mr. Secretary, the reporter did not deflect. He asked the fraud task force about $420 million of public money. If that is a waste of your time, you may want to check the banner, because it is possible you are at the wrong event.

pt.title: A matéria principal: a força-tarefa antifraude prefere que você não pergunte sobre a prisão de US$ 420 milhões
pt.dek: O governo foi a Minnesota caçar fraudes. Deixa para trás uma prisão de US$ 495,6 milhões que havia sido oferecida ao estado por US$ 75 milhões, um relatório do órgão de controle com “desperdício” no título, dois cidadãos mortos e um secretário do Tesouro que chamou a pergunta de perda de tempo.

de.title: Die Hauptgeschichte: Die Betrugs-Taskforce hätte lieber keine Fragen zum 420-Millionen-Dollar-Gefängnis
de.dek: Die Regierung kam nach Minnesota, um Betrug zu jagen. Sie hinterlässt ein Gefängnis für 495,6 Millionen Dollar, das dem Bundesstaat für 75 Millionen angeboten worden war, einen Prüfbericht mit „Verschwendung“ im Titel, zwei tote Bürger und einen Finanzminister, der die Frage Zeitverschwendung nannte.
